cognate: Arm. ayr (aṙn) = Gk ἀνήρ (*h₂nér-); Arm. anown = Gk ὄνομα (*h₁nómn̥); Arm. ēr = Gk ἦν (*h₁es-, impf.); the relative pronoun in the dative in both (Arm. orowm, Gk τῷ) is not cognate but has the same function
drift_or_renewal: none in the core; ON 'maðr er nefndr N' (BS-8ad62) and OE 'N is mīn nama' (BS-0ee8c etc.) give the same introduction with renewed verb or possessive syntax and are not part of the claim
shared_syntax: [*h₂nér- (+ attributes)] + relative pronoun in the dative of possession + *h₁nómn̥ (nom.) + past of *h₁es- + proper name: 'a man ..., to whom the name was N'; also the short type 'N by name' (Arm. 'Maštocʻ anown', acc. of respect, like Gk οὔνομα)
context: Prose historiography, at the point where a new character comes into the narrative: Łazar brings in Mesrop Maštocʻ's father, Herodotus brings in Demonax, Deioces, Mitrobates. In both traditions the formula is a fixed device of the genre (16 such units in the Armenian historians, 15 in Herodotus) and stands in the same place in the sentence, after the man's description
phrase: *h₂nér ... kʷo-/yo- (DAT) *h₁nómn̥ *h₁es-t N, 'a man to whom the name was N'
note: The cognates line up and the construction (name + dative possessor + 'be') is old and widespread: Lat. 'nomen Mercurio est mihi' in Plautus (found by search); Hitt. 'Appu-ša ŠUM-an-šet' at the start of the Appu tale and OIr. 'Mac Dathó a ainm' are recalled. But it is also everyday language, and Classical Armenian may have taken it as a calque from Biblical Greek (Lk 1:27 ἀνδρὶ ᾧ ὄνομα Ἰωσήφ = Arm. aṙn orowm anown Yovsēpʻ, recalled). So the case for independent inheritance is weak: the claim is that the two daughters share the same wording, built from cognate words, in the same narrative slot.

near_miss.lead: pouring tears: Arm. artasowacʻ vtaks hełeal ~ Hom. δάκρυ χέουσαι
near_miss.why_not: artasowkʻ ~ δάκρυ are cognate, but Arm. hełowm is not cognate with χέω. 'Shedding tears' is universal, and here it is in Biblical style; Homer's 'night and day' has no Armenian match in this passage

near_miss.lead: day and night merism: Arm. i towē ew i gišeri (tiw < *dyew-, gišer < *wekʷsper-) ~ Gk ἦμαρ ... ἕσπερα
near_miss.why_not: the Greek line is not a merism ('the day is far gone, evening will be colder'). 'By day and by night' is a generic merism and Biblical in Armenian (cf. zcʻayg ew zcʻerek, BS-1c0a6)

anchors: xcl:MH_1_2_12_Movses_Khor ed. page 2156 - PDF page 413 (word id 66878)
near_miss.lead: gods swear by a cold spring (Styx): Arm. dikʻn erdnowin (dikʻ ~ θεοί)
near_miss.why_not: the Armenian Geography takes this from Greek sources (Ptolemy/Pappus), so it is borrowed lore, not inheritance. The partners (ON naming with water, AV name of the waters) are not congruent

near_miss.lead: summon to the court: Arm. i dowrn kočʻel ~ Serb. u dvor dozivati (*dʰwer- 'door' > 'court')
near_miss.why_not: the shift door > court is parallel, but the Armenian 'royal Porte' is an Iranian model (dar), the Serbian dvor is a domestic courtyard where sisters-in-law call each other, and the verbs are not cognate. The bundle also rests on a mis-lemmatized 'nēr'
